chunks.text: II-A Diffusion models, bridges and inverse problems Widely used denoising diffusion models [ 27 ] and their score-based formulations [ 28 ] add Gaussian noise according to a prescribed variance schedule. Subsequent work has improved sampling [ 29 ] and network parameterization [ 30 ] . Restoration-oriented methods also redesign the trajectory. For example, ResShift introduces residual shifting to reduce the number of sampling steps [ 31 ] . Restoration bridges connect clean and degraded image distributions. Schrödinger bridge formulations connect prescribed endpoint distributions [ 32 ] , with I 2 SB applying this principle to image restoration [ 21 ] . Other formulations use direct endpoint interpolation [ 33 ] or mean-reverting stochastic differential equations [ 34 ] . More recent developments target spatial adaptation and efficiency. RDBM uses endpoint residuals to modulate noise injection and removal across image regions [ 35 ] , while E-Bridge shortens the trajectory and learns a consistency-based mapping for single-step restoration [ 36 ] . System-Embedded Diffusion Bridge Models incorporate the forward system explicitly, embedding a known linear operator and noise covariance into a matrix-valued SDE under an additive Gaussian measurement model [ 37 ] . Another class of methods adapts a pretrained diffusion prior to the observation. DDRM uses the singular-value decomposition of the forward operator [ 38 ] , whereas DPS introduces an approximate likelihood score [ 22 ] . DPS supports Poisson measurement noise while retaining a Gaussian diffusion prior. IRBridge transfers pretrained generative priors to restoration bridges by relating processes with a common endpoint distribution [ 39 ] . Non-Gaussian constructions extend the choice of diffusion distributions. Xie et al. formulate diffusion denoising for Gaussian, Gamma, and Poisson corruption with a unified training strategy [ 23 ] .

Learning to Jump uses count thinning and reverse count thickening for generative modeling [ 40 ] , while Star-Shaped DDPM develops non-Gaussian models within exponential families [ 41 ] . In statistical inference, data thinning splits observations from convolution-closed distributions, including Gaussian, Poisson, and Gamma laws, into independent components [ 42 ] . Gamma Bridge indexes a speckle-denoising trajectory by the number of looks [ 24 ] . p p -Bridge extends this measurement-indexed formulation to the Gaussian point and the Poisson-to-Gamma continuum, using a common superposition construction and a single exponent-conditioned network. IV Experiments We evaluate p p -Bridge on synthetic noise spanning the exponent and severity axes, followed by real fluorescence microscopy and SAR data. The experiments examine exponent mismatch and conditioning, compare restoration methods, and evaluate noise parameter estimation and robustness to exponent. IV-A Experimental setup Training data. We use a pool of 1,100 1{,}100 clean natural images from BSDS500 and DIV2K [ 53 , 54 ] , with 256 × 256 256\times 256 training crops. Clean intensities are mapped to 𝒳 = [ 0.05 , 1 ] \mathcal{X}=[0.05,1] using the intensity offset. Noisy observations are generated from the corresponding Tweedie model. Synthetic evaluation. We evaluate on 64 64 held-out crops with noise exponents p data ∈ { 1 , 1.25 , 1.5 , 1.75 , 2 } p_{\mathrm{data}}\in\{1,1.25,1.5,1.75,2\} and severities η ∈ { 0.25 , 0.5 , 1 } \eta\in\{0.25,0.5,1\} (mild, moderate, and severe). Each fixed-exponent model is tested across all five exponents, with results averaged over three corruption seeds. Comparisons with external methods use p data ∈ { 1 , 1.5 , 2 } p_{\mathrm{data}}\in\{1,1.5,2\} . Real-data evaluation. Noise calibration covers 12 12 FMD fluorescence microscopy configurations [ 11 ] and three SAR sensors: miniSAR, FARAD-X, and TerraSAR-X.

Restoration comparisons use three FMD configurations, following the prior protocol, and all three SAR sensors. For each FMD configuration, we use 19 19 fields for fine-tuning over 20,000 20{,}000 steps and one held-out field for evaluation. Dataset-specific preprocessing and calibration are described in the corresponding experimental subsections. Evaluation metrics. We report PSNR and SSIM against clean synthetic images or the FMD frame-average reference. The supplementary sampling-budget study also reports dark-region log-RMSE ( Table S2 ). For real SAR, where clean references are unavailable, we report the ratio-image measures ℳ \mathcal{M} [ 55 ] and RIS \mathrm{RIS} [ 56 ] alongside visual comparisons. Model and training. We use a UNet with time embedding, containing 15.19 15.19 M parameters for fixed-exponent models and 15.28 15.28 M with exponent conditioning. The conditional model samples p p uniformly from { 1 , 1.05 , … , 2 } \{1,1.05,\ldots,2\} per micro-batch. Each bridge model is trained once for 50,000 50{,}000 steps with global batch size 24 24 , 1,000 1{,}000 warmup steps, and cosine learning-rate decay from 10 − 4 10^{-4} to 10 − 7 10^{-7} . Loss weights are fixed at ( λ rec , λ mom , λ cons ) = ( 10 , 1 , 5 ) (\lambda_{\mathrm{rec}},\lambda_{\mathrm{mom}},\lambda_{\mathrm{cons}})=(10,1,5) . Implementation details are provided in the supplement. Noise calibration. We compare different noise models by matching their relative noise at a reference intensity. We use μ ref = 0.464864 \mu_{\mathrm{ref}}=0.464864 , the mean intensity of the offset training pool, and define the noise level η \eta as the ratio of noise standard deviation to this reference intensity. The required measurement index is then ν obs ​ ( p ) = η − 2 ​ μ ref p − 2 . \nu_{\mathrm{obs}}(p)=\eta^{-2}\mu_{\mathrm{ref}}^{\,p-2}. (21) This calibration matches noise levels at μ ref \mu_{\mathrm{ref}} .

Away from this reference, relative noise increases towards darker regions for p < 2 p<2 , whereas it remains constant across intensities for p = 2 p=2 . Figure 4 illustrates how the noise exponent affects the spatial distribution of relative noise. Inference and severity transfer. Unless otherwise stated, p p -Bridge uses deterministic sampling with five network evaluations. Models trained at severe noise ( η = 1 \eta=1 ) are also evaluated at moderate and mild noise without retraining. For a less noisy input, sampling starts at its corresponding measurement index within the trained range. For real-image evaluation, calibrated noise-plane coordinates ( p , ν ) (p,\nu) configure the bridge and select the starting point for denoising. IV-B Behaviour along the exponent axis The cost of a mismatched exponent. Figure 5 compares models trained at different noise exponents on the same noisy inputs. Each column fixes p data p_{\mathrm{data}} , allowing direct comparison with the matched model. At severe noise, applying a Gamma-trained model ( p model = 2 p_{\mathrm{model}}=2 ) to Poisson data ( p data = 1 p_{\mathrm{data}}=1 ) reduces PSNR by 4.40 ​ dB 4.40\,\mathrm{dB} , the largest loss across the three noise levels. The reverse mismatch costs approximately 3.3 ​ dB 3.3\,\mathrm{dB} , showing that the two directions are not equally harmful. Across the mismatched pairs in the p ∈ { 1 , 1.5 , 2 } p\in\{1,1.5,2\} subgrid, the average loss at severe noise is 2.00 ​ dB 2.00\,\mathrm{dB} . On the 5 × 5 5\times 5 evaluation grid, the matched model achieves the highest PSNR in every column at all three noise levels. Performance differences remain observable even between adjacent exponents separated by 0.25 0.25 , indicating sensitivity to relatively small mismatches. When the noise exponent is unknown, we evaluate each fixed-exponent model by its lowest PSNR across the tested noise exponents. Table II shows that p = 1.5 p=1.5 maximizes this worst-case PSNR at severe and moderate noise, reaching 21.339 21.339 and 23.112 ​ dB 23.112\,\mathrm{dB} , respectively. At mild noise, the optimum shifts to p = 1.75 p=1.75 , with 26.336 ​ dB 26.336\,\mathrm{dB} . Thus, an interior exponent offers the strongest worst-case performance among the tested fixed models, but no single exponent is optimal at every noise level. We therefore use p = 1.5 p=1.5 as a fixed-model baseline and next examine whether conditioning on the noise exponent improves robustness across the full range. The p p -conditional network. To cover different noise exponents with a single model, we condition the network on p p through an embedding alongside the time embedding. During training, p p is sampled uniformly from { 1 , 1.05 , … , 2 } \{1,1.05,\ldots,2\} for each micro-batch.

Table II compares the conditional network with fixed-exponent models in terms of worst-case PSNR across noise exponents. Using estimated rather than true exponents, the conditional network improves over the fixed p = 1.5 p=1.5 model by 0.921 0.921 , 1.525 1.525 , and 1.413 ​ dB 1.413\,\mathrm{dB} at severe, moderate, and mild noise, respectively. Against the best fixed-exponent model at each severity, the gains are 0.921 0.921 , 1.525 1.525 , and 1.099 ​ dB 1.099\,\mathrm{dB} . The smaller mild-noise gain reflects the stronger p = 1.75 p=1.75 baseline. We also compare the conditional network with an oracle-selected set of five specialist models, one for each tested exponent. At severe, moderate, and mild noise, the specialists achieve minimum PSNRs across the tested exponents of 22.254 22.254 , 24.631 24.631 , and 27.431 ​ dB 27.431\,\mathrm{dB} , compared with 22.260 22.260 , 24.637 24.637 , and 27.435 ​ dB 27.435\,\mathrm{dB} for the conditional network using estimated exponents. The minimum PSNRs differ by at most 0.006 ​ dB 0.006\,\mathrm{dB} across the three noise levels. Using estimated exponents yields nearly identical minimum PSNR to using the true exponents. In Table II , the differences between these two inputs to the same conditional network are 0.000 0.000 , + 0.002 +0.002 , and − 0.001 ​ dB -0.001\,\mathrm{dB} at severe, moderate, and mild noise, respectively. To verify that the network uses the exponent input, we vary the conditioning exponent while keeping the data exponent fixed. The matching exponent achieves the highest PSNR for all five tested data exponents at every noise level, confirming that the conditioning input affects restoration performance. IV-C Comparison We compare p p -Bridge with baseline methods on synthetic images, FMD fluorescence microscopy, and real SAR data. We report PSNR and SSIM for synthetic and FMD images, and ratio-image metrics with visual comparisons for SAR. Synthetic images.

Table III reports results for nine combinations of noise exponent and severity. Compared with external baselines, conditional p p -Bridge achieves the highest PSNR in eight settings and the highest SSIM in all nine. Noise2VST leads only in PSNR at mild noise with p data = 1 p_{\mathrm{data}}=1 , by 0.02 ​ dB 0.02\,\mathrm{dB} . Improvements over VIRNet are small but consistent, ranging from 0.06 0.06 to 0.09 ​ dB 0.09\,\mathrm{dB} . Performance also varies less across noise exponents. At severe noise, PSNR drops by 0.13 ​ dB 0.13\,\mathrm{dB} from p data = 1 p_{\mathrm{data}}=1 to 2 2 , compared with 0.94 ​ dB 0.94\,\mathrm{dB} for Noise2VST. Figure 6 provides visual comparisons. Fluorescence microscopy (FMD). Table IV reports results on three FMD configurations. Conditional p p -Bridge achieves the highest mean SSIM ( 0.912 0.912 ) and the second-highest mean PSNR ( 31.76 ​ dB 31.76\,\mathrm{dB} ), compared with 31.83 ​ dB 31.83\,\mathrm{dB} for VIRNet. The PSNR ranking varies by configuration. Our model trails VIRNet by 0.11 0.11 and 0.23 ​ dB 0.23\,\mathrm{dB} on CF-FISH and CF-MICE, respectively, but leads on TP-MICE with 32.68 ​ dB 32.68\,\mathrm{dB} , a 0.13 ​ dB 0.13\,\mathrm{dB} gain. For SSIM, it ranks first on CF-FISH and shares first place with VIRNet on the other two configurations. Its mean PSNR also exceeds I 2 SB by 0.61 ​ dB 0.61\,\mathrm{dB} . Noise parameters are calibrated from training-field frame stacks. All comparisons follow the same protocol. The table distinguishes fine-tuned methods from those transferred without fine-tuning. Among the ranked methods, p p -Bridge achieves the lowest mean ℳ \mathcal{M} and RIS \mathrm{RIS} ( 19.4 / 35.3 19.4/35.3 ), followed by NAFNet ( 22.0 / 37.7 22.0/37.7 ).

It ranks first on both metrics for miniSAR and TerraSAR-X, second for FARAD-X, where NAFNet scores lower by 0.6 0.6 and 2.7 2.7 , respectively. Figure 8 complements these ratio-image metrics with visual comparisons of noise removal and detail preservation. Noise calibration is detailed in the supplement. Table VI summarizes the component ablations of the conditional model. Each variant changes one setting while keeping the others fixed. Training-side variants are retrained with the same data and budget, whereas inference-only variants reuse the full model’s checkpoint. Loss weighting and index schedule. Measurement-dependent weighting and a linear index schedule reduce PSNR by 0.345 0.345 and 0.268 ​ dB 0.268\,\mathrm{dB} , respectively. Although the mean reconstruction weight is unchanged, measurement-dependent weighting assigns greater weight to cleaner states. Likewise, a linear schedule allocates fewer training steps near the noisy observation than a geometric schedule over the same index range. These results support the use of constant weighting and geometric spacing to emphasize noisy states under a fixed training budget. Regularization and reverse update.

At five network evaluations, removing consistency regularization and replacing the reverse mixture with direct prediction reduce PSNR by 0.210 0.210 and 0.186 ​ dB 0.186\,\mathrm{dB} , respectively. These losses increase to 0.452 0.452 and 1.654 ​ dB 1.654\,\mathrm{dB} at 25 25 evaluations. At one evaluation, no reverse update is applied, so the two samplers produce identical outputs. Removing consistency regularization changes PSNR by only 0.004 ​ dB 0.004\,\mathrm{dB} . By comparison, removing moment regularization or exponent-dependent loss weighting reduces PSNR by only 0.010 0.010 and 0.012 ​ dB 0.012\,\mathrm{dB} , respectively. Figure 9 illustrates the structural degradation of ablations. No-projection result remains visually close to the full model. Output-range projection. With matched exponents, removing projection changes PSNR by at most 0.001 ​ dB 0.001\,\mathrm{dB} at one, five, and 25 25 network evaluations. Its benefit is more evident when the conditioning exponent is below the data exponent. For Gamma noise ( p data = 2 p_{\mathrm{data}}=2 ) with the conditioning exponent set to 1 1 , removing projection reduces PSNR by 0.223 0.223 , 0.168 0.168 , and 0.139 ​ dB 0.139\,\mathrm{dB} , respectively. Projection therefore provides a modest benefit under exponent mismatch, with little effect on matched-noise performance. We first examine how accurately the exponent must be estimated to retain the benefit of conditioning. Table VII compares the conditional network with the fixed p = 1.5 p=1.5 model under worst-case errors satisfying | p ^ − p data | ≤ δ |\hat{p}-p_{\mathrm{data}}|\leq\delta . At δ = 0.25 \delta=0.25 , the PSNR gains remain 0.830 0.830 – 1.311 ​ dB 1.311\,\mathrm{dB} across the three noise levels, only 0.09 0.09 – 0.21 ​ dB 0.21\,\mathrm{dB} below exact conditioning. At δ = 0.5 \delta=0.5 , the gains decrease to 0.107 0.107 – 0.184 ​ dB 0.184\,\mathrm{dB} but remain positive. Without an error constraint over the tested exponent range, the conditional model falls below the fixed baseline by 1.707 1.707 – 1.863 ​ dB 1.863\,\mathrm{dB} . Thus, errors within 0.25 0.25 preserve most of the conditioning benefit in these tests. Figure 10 shows how this cost varies with intensity. Overestimating the exponent concentrates excess error in dark regions, whereas underestimating it affects bright regions. The observed estimator errors remain within δ = 0.25 \delta=0.25 . V Conclusion p p -Bridge connects statistical noise modeling with the design of a denoising trajectory. Measurement accumulation provides the common bridge structure, while exponent conditioning adapts the learned prediction to the noise law. The experiments show that this adaptation matters beyond selecting a noise level. Fixed-exponent models lose accuracy under mismatched noise laws, whereas a shared conditional network achieves cross-exponent robustness comparable to oracle-selected specialists. Using estimated exponents leaves this robustness nearly unchanged, and moderate conditioning errors preserve most of the benefit. Results on synthetic images, fluorescence microscopy, and SAR further support the usefulness of the formulation across imaging regimes. Together, these findings support adapting to different Tweedie noise models by making the noise law an explicit condition within a shared restoration model, without a separate checkpoint for each exponent.
